My name is Amy, and I am a resident of Sullivan, ME. I am writing in support of LD 1128.
I am on a fertility adventure. This is a phrase I've used to find light in a dark tunnel. I was born and raised on the coast of Maine, playing in the blueberry barrens with my cousins. Now, at 39 years old, I am trying to start a family with my husband, an oyster farmer born and raised in Maine.
We lead active, healthy lives and still struggle with unexplained infertility. Navigating the medical system with busy lives can feel like a sea squall with rain and winds closing in on us. Shame, fear, and anxiety are only a few feelings I've had during this infertility journey. Being self-employed oyster farmers makes health insurance very expensive and challenging.
Without the care and presence of my naturopath doctor, I strongly believe we would have given up hope for a family a long time ago. My ND offers their time and patience and responds with thoughtfulness as my body changes and flows through my cycles. They unturned every stone on the path to what will someday lead to a healthy pregnancy. I can rely on regular scheduled meetings and make informed and precise adjustments to treatments in real time with a human touch.
My naturopath has offered me tools to feel confident in our treatment plan, they support the use of prescription medications with a balanced approach that feels comprehensive, safe, and well-researched. We are about to begin IVF treatments, and our naturopath is helping prepare my body for invasive surgery through these aforementioned balanced treatments to help reduce the side effects of serious medications. This collaborative approach feels safe, sustainable, and empowering.
I urge your committee to pass the bill LD 1128, and thank you for allowing me to send in this testimony.

my blood for two years. But it was a naturopath's skill, insight and a thorough 90-minute appointment that finally put me on the path to recovery.

In cases like mine, a prescription medication can be the most effective and safest treatment. But
when patients are experiencing serious, acute conditions, delays in accessing these medications
can result in severe adverse outcomes.
Naturopathic doctors are trained on a much broader formulary than they are allowed to use here in Maine. And maybe they would administer more vaccines if they were permitted to -- every

and with the rights already granted to naturopathic doctors in New Hampshire and Vermont.
Maine's caregivers -- all of them - need every tool possible to treat those most in need.

About Naturopathic Physicians

What is a Naturopathic Physician?

Naturopathic physicians (NDs) combine the wisdom of nature with the rigors of modern science.

They focus

on holistic, proactive prevention and comprehensive diagnosis and treatment. Naturopathic medicine facilitates

the body's inherent ability to restore and maintain optimal health.

NDs are recognized as primary care physicians in many states. They work in private practices, hospitals, clinics, and community health centers. Among the most common ailments they treat are allergies, chronic pain, digestive issues, hormonal imbalances, obesity, heart disease, fertility problems, menopause, adrenal fatigue, cancer, and
fibromyalgia.

Naturopathic physicians are trained in a variety of diagnostic and therapeutic modalities. They include: clinical and laboratory diagnostic testing, nutritional medicine, botanical medicine, naturopathic physical medicine (including naturopathic manipulative therapy), immunizations, counseling, minor surgery, homeopathy, acupuncture, intravenous and injection therapy, and naturopathic obstetrics (natural childbirth). While NDs are trained to prescribe drugs, they emphasize the use of natural healing agents.

Principles of Naturopathic Medicine
The following principles are the foundation of naturopathic medical practice:
o The Healing Power of Nature: Naturopathic medicine recognizes an inherent self~healing process in people that is ordered and intelligent. Naturopathic physicians act to identify and remove obstacles to healing and
recovery.
o Identify and Treat the Causes: NDs seek to identify and remove the underlying causes of illness rather than to merely eliminate or suppress symptoms.
o First Do No Harm: NDs follow three guidelines to avoid harming the patient:
~ Utilize methods and medicinal substances which minimize the risk of harmful side effects, using the least force necessary to diagnose and treat;
0 Avoid when possible the harmful suppression of symptoms; and
0 Acknowledge, respect, and work with individuals' self-healing process.
o Doctor as Teacher: NDs educate their patients and encourage self-responsibility for health. v Treat the Whole Person: NDs treat each patient by taking into account individual physical,
mental, emotional, genetic, environmental, social, and other factors. Since total health also includes spiritual health, naturopathic physicians encourage individuals to pursue their personal spiritual development.
~ Prevention: NDs emphasize the prevention of disease by assessing risk factors, heredity and susceptibility to disease, and by making appropriate interventions in partnership with their patients to prevent illness.

Naturopathic Physicians Licensing Examination (NPLEX) is an independent, nonprofit organization whose purpose is to develop valid and reliable licensing examinations. The
NPLEX has been developed in accordance with accepted psychometric standards and principles, encompassing practice analysis, exam blueprint development, item writer
training, subject matter expert review, post-test psychometric analysis and standard setting via the Angoff method.

The examinations developed by NPLEX are primarily case based, consisting of clinical summaries followed by several questions pertaining to the patient's case. The integrated
nature of this type of testing ensures the examinee demonstrates concurrent mastery of the
competencies tested. The NPLEX Council of Exam Chairs oversees the exam development
process.

THE PART I - BIOMEDICAL SCIENCE EXAMINATION

The Part I -- Biomedical Science Examination evaluates the foundational knowledge and

skills required for clinical training. Taken after completion of all biomedical science

coursework at an accredited naturopathic medical program, the 200-question Part I -

Biomedical Science Examination evaluates comprehensive knowledge in seven specific

biomedical areas: anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, genetics, microbiology, immunology,

and pathology.

~

THE PART II - CLINICAL SCIENCE EXAMINATIONS

The Part ll - Core Clinical Science Examination evaluates the advanced knowledge and clinical decision--making skills essential for safe and effective practice as a naturopathic physician. After successful passage of Part I and graduation from a CNME-accredited naturopathic program, candidates are eligible to take Part ll.

The 400-question NPLEX Part II - Core Clinical Science Examination evaluates nine core
areas including physical and clinical diagnosis, lab and imaging diagnostics, pharmacology, emergency medicine, clinical nutrition, physical medicine, psychology, botanical medicine and homeopathy.

Do naturopathic doctors prescribe medication?
Licensed naturopathic doctors (NDs) are trained as primary care providers to diagnose,
prevent, and treat acute and chronic illness. NDs complete rigorous education in
pharmaceutical drugs during their four-year, science--based medical education, and they
may prescribe medications when indicated as allowed by state regulations. However, naturopathic doctors typically don't prescribe drugs at the first sign of symptoms or trouble. Instead, NDs choose to work with natural, less invasive therapies without strong side effect
profiles before reaching for the prescription pad. They support and enhance a patient's innate capacity for healing with evidence-based therapies such as lifestyle modification,
clinical nutrition, botanical medicine, and behavioral medicine, to name a few.

Pharmacology education and training
Pharmacology is taught through a series of courses that build upon each other through an
ND's medical education. This training is reinforced through a minimum of 1,200 hours of
hands-on, clinical training. Naturopathic medical programs are accredited and are recognized by the United States Department of Education. Pharmacology is an essential part of the Naturopathic Physicians Licensing Examination (NPLEX), the passage of which is required before a doctor of naturopathic medicine can be licensed or regulated by a
state/province.

As part of the pharmacology curriculum, naturopathic doctors learn both medical and clinical pharmacology. They study primary therapeutic uses, mechanisms of action, potential adverse effects, and drug/drug interactions of medicines commonly encountered, including prescription drugs, controlled substances, and over the counter (OTC) medications.
Additionally, they learn how to prescribe and manage pharmaceuticals for the most common
presenting concerns in primary care medicine.
While pharmacology coursework is comparable to that taught in conventional medical
schools, NDs receive additional training and focus in two important areas:
1. Botanical or herb/drug and supplement/drug interactions. Seventy-five
percent of Americans regularly take herbs and dietary supplements, and they don't always inform their primary care doctor. Naturopathic doctors complete approximately 130 classroom hours of botanical medicine education. This

deficiencies of vital nutrients with ongoing use. These include medicines prescribed for acid reflux, heartburn, cholesterol, and more. Naturopathic doctors are expert at identifying signs of nutrient depletion, and apply their extensive knowledge of clinical nutrition and botanical medicine to help reverse these harmful side effects.

NDs are also trained to identify when and whether a patient is overmedicated, and when prescriptions, OTC medicines, and supplements can be tapered off or discontinued.

Naturopathic doctors prescribe drugs based on available evidence, clinical experience,

patient preference, and the Therapeutic Order. They match the patient's level of health and

Good afternoon Committee Chair Senator Bailey, Co-chair Representative Gramlich and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of LD 1128 today.
My name is Wendy Sincyr, I am a RN and I reside in Embden. I am writing in support of LD 1128. I am writing as a patient of a Naturopathic Doctor and as someone who works in health care. I first learned of Naturopathic Doctors during nursing school at KVCC in 2016. I have a complex health history and chronic health conditions. I decided to visit a Naturopathic Doctor to explore whether there were some more holistic and natural treatments for my chronic health conditions. I was highly impressed with the Naturopathic Doctors' explanation of the inter-connectedness of the conditions, the exact internal mechanisms at play, how they could be treated in a more natural way and the mechanism of action of those therapies. I am confident and comfortable with my Naturopathic Doctor prescribing medications and supplements because she understands the actions and interactions between medications and supplements. I am more likely to agree to a new medication or supplement prescribed by my Naturopathic Doctor because she explains the need for it, the mechanism of action in the body, how it will be beneficial and all the interactions taken into consideration before choosing that medication. We have been working on getting to the root causes of my chronic health conditions, and have made great improvement in my overall health. Unfortunately, there are some medications that my Naturopathic Doctor can not adjust, I must see my primary care physician for that. Which means another doctors visit, extra time and extra cost. For one of my chronic conditions, I had to see yet another doctor every month, 50 miles one-way from my home, for just that one condition and one medication. Respectfully,
Wendy Sincyr, RN
